facts.statehood_note: Ratified the U.S. Constitution; as the ninth state to ratify, New Hampshire's vote made the Constitution the law of the land.

symbols.name: Ladybug (also called the ladybird or lady beetle)

facts.name_origin: Captain John Mason, the colony's founder, named it after his home county in England, Hampshire.

government.chambers: New Hampshire Senate (24 senators) and New Hampshire House of Representatives (400 representatives, the second-largest representative body in the United States); all are elected every two years.
government.executive: Governor (2-year term) and the Executive Council: five councilors, each representing a district. Unlike councils in other states that only advise, New Hampshire's council decides together with the governor whom to appoint to lead state agencies and to serve as judges.
government.courts: New Hampshire Supreme Court (five justices). All New Hampshire judges are appointed by the governor and Executive Council instead of being elected.
government.local: 10 counties, 13 cities, and 221 towns. Each town holds a town meeting at least once a year, where voters discuss and vote on local issues.
government.constitution: Constitution of 1784, the second-oldest state constitution in the United States, changed many times since. New Hampshire wrote the first state constitution in January 1776. In 1784 only white men who owned property could vote.
government.kid_line: "It shall be the duty of the legislators and magistrates, in all future periods of this government, to cherish the interest of literature and the sciences, and all seminaries and public schools" (New Hampshire Constitution, Part Second, Article 83)

long_ago.about: The Abenaki homeland, N'dakinna, includes what is now New Hampshire. Each wigwam housed one family, and crops grew around the edges of the village. Around 3,000 years ago they began growing corn, beans, and squash together, and they taught English settlers to tap trees for maple syrup and to make snowshoes and canoes.

An Abenaki people of the Merrimack River valley, as many as 12,000 strong in the 1600s, led by the sachem Passaconaway. Abenaki people from all over the region gathered at Amoskeag Falls on the Merrimack every spring and fall to catch fish.
An Abenaki band led by the sachem Wehanownowit. In summer they lived and farmed where the Squamscott and Exeter rivers meet, and many Abenaki bands met there to fish for salmon.
Along with the Pennacook, these Algonquian-speaking Abenaki nations lived in the area before Europeans came.

first_peoples.today_note: Descendants of New Hampshire's Abenaki people still live in the state today, gathering to sing traditional songs and making traditional crafts; for example, potter Vicki Blanchard is a citizen of the Nulhegan Band of the Coosuk Abenaki. Many New Hampshire place names come from the Abenaki language, and the Kancamagus Highway and Mount Kancamagus are named for a Pennacook sachem.
sites: Amoskeag Falls on the Merrimack River in Manchester, a great Abenaki fishing place for thousands of years, where archaeologists still find ancient Abenaki artifacts.

history.event: Indigenous people live near today's Keene, according to archaeological digs in 2009.
The Abenaki begin farming, planting corn, beans, and squash in addition to hunting, fishing, and gathering.
European visitors bring diseases like smallpox. Thousands of Abenaki people become sick and many die. The Pennacook sachem Passaconaway urges his people to live in peace with the English.
English settlers led by David Thomson set up a fishing station at Odiorne Point in Rye, the first permanent European settlement in New Hampshire. Dover is also founded that year.
John Wheelwright's group signs a deed with the Squamscott sachem Wehanownowit to settle at Exeter. The deed says the Squamscott still have the right to hunt and fish there.
Richard Waldron of Dover invites Abenaki and Wampanoag people to a feast, but it is a trick: the Wampanoag are arrested, and many are enslaved and shipped to the West Indies.
Abenaki fighters led by Kancamagus, Passaconaway's grandson, attack Dover and kill Waldron. As English settlers take more land, many Abenaki move north and west.
In January, New Hampshire writes the first state constitution and becomes the first colony to declare independence from Great Britain.

Twenty enslaved men in Portsmouth, including Prince Whipple, petition the state to end slavery, using the same arguments for freedom that the colonists used against Britain. The government ignores them.
New Hampshire's constitution takes effect; it is still in use today. At first only white men who owned property can vote.
On June 21, New Hampshire becomes the ninth state to ratify the U.S. Constitution, which makes the Constitution the law of the land.
Ona Judge escapes slavery in President George Washington's household and reaches Portsmouth by ship. She lives the rest of her life in New Hampshire and is never recaptured.

John P. Hale of Dover speaks out against slavery and later becomes the first U.S. senator to run for office as an abolitionist. In 1853 Amos Tuck and friends meet in Exeter to form a new antislavery party, the Republicans.
New Hampshire sends 18 volunteer regiments to the Union Army. The 'Fighting Fifth' helps stop a Confederate attack at Gettysburg, and nurse Harriet Dame cares for wounded soldiers on the battlefield.

trailblazers.name: Passaconaway
trailblazers.text: Passaconaway, whose name means 'child of the bear,' led the Pennacook people of the Merrimack Valley as the English arrived. His people believed he had special powers. He urged the Abenaki to live peacefully with the settlers to keep his people safe and protect their culture.

trailblazers.name: Wentworth Cheswell
trailblazers.group: Black American man, town leader and patriot
trailblazers.text: Wentworth Cheswell of Newmarket is thought to be the first Black person elected to public office in America, as town constable in 1768. He later served as town clerk, selectman, and representative, and fought at the Battle of Saratoga. His grandfather Richard had bought his own freedom from slavery.

trailblazers.name: Prince Whipple
trailblazers.group: African-born Black American man, freedom fighter
trailblazers.text: Born in Africa and enslaved as a child, Prince Whipple was held by Portsmouth merchant William Whipple, a patriot leader, and fought beside him in the Revolutionary War. In 1779 he signed the petition asking New Hampshire to end slavery. He was freed in 1784, and his wife Dinah and sister-in-law Rebecca opened a school in their Portsmouth home.

trailblazers.name: Ona Judge
trailblazers.text: Born into slavery at George Washington's Mount Vernon, Ona Judge escaped from the president's house in Philadelphia in 1796 and sailed to Portsmouth. The Washingtons kept trying to get her back, so she moved to Greenland, New Hampshire. She married John Staines, raised three children, and was never recaptured.

trailblazers.name: Harriet Wilson
trailblazers.text: Harriet Wilson of Milford was the first Black person to publish a novel in the United States, in 1859. Her book, based on her own hard childhood working for a cruel family, showed that Black people faced racism in the North too. (Its title uses an old, offensive word.) A statue of her was created in 2006.

trailblazers.name: Christa McAuliffe
trailblazers.text: A social studies teacher at Concord High School, Christa McAuliffe was chosen from more than 11,000 applicants to be NASA's first Teacher in Space. She died with her crewmates when the space shuttle Challenger exploded after takeoff on January 28, 1986. She often said, 'I touch the future. I teach.'

landforms: White Mountains, with 48 peaks over 4,000 feet
Mount Washington (6,288 feet), the tallest mountain in the Northeast
Notches (mountain passes) such as Crawford Notch and Franconia Notch
Granite bedrock under almost half the state
A short Atlantic seacoast with hills shaped by glaciers, like Little Boar's Head
waters: Connecticut, Merrimack, and Saco rivers, which all begin in New Hampshire (the 'Mother of Rivers')
Lake Winnipesaukee (69 square miles), the largest lake in the state
More than 40,000 miles of rivers and streams
Great Bay and the Piscataqua River near Portsmouth
geography.regions: Glaciers shaped New Hampshire's lakes and valleys; the state is often divided into seven tourist regions, including the Lakes Region and the White Mountains, and most people live in the south.

ecosystems.name: Northern forests
ecosystems.about: Forests cover much of the state and are home to black bears, lynx, moose, bats, purple finches, eagles, turtles, salamanders, and toads. In spring, sugar maples are tapped for sap: about 40 gallons of sap make 1 gallon of maple syrup.

ecosystems.name: Alpine tundra on Mount Washington
ecosystems.about: Above the trees it is cold with strong winds, and few animals live there, though bobcats, rattlesnakes, and eagles can be found.

ecosystems.name: Rivers and falls
ecosystems.about: Fast rivers like the Merrimack were rich fishing grounds; an Abenaki legend said there were so many fish you could walk across the river on their backs.

science.weather: New Hampshire has four strong seasons: hot, humid summers and cold, snowy winters. Blizzards and nor'easters bring heavy snow (the blizzards of 1888 and 1978 dropped several feet), hurricanes sometimes sweep up the coast, and floods have hit cities on the Merrimack River. Mount Washington is known for some of the worst weather in the world and once held the record for the fastest wind ever measured on Earth.
science.resources: Granite, forests (the British king once claimed the biggest pines for ship masts), and fast rivers that powered textile mills like the giant Amoskeag Manufacturing Company in Manchester. Today the economy includes high-tech businesses, financial services, education, manufacturing, and tourism.
science.highlight: Mount Washington's extreme weather: the summit has its own climate, and it can be freezing and windy at the top while it is hot on the coast. Also, the Old Man of the Mountain, a granite face in Franconia Notch, fell on May 3, 2003, a lesson in how ice and weather wear down rock.

g3_ss.title: New Hampshire's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Town meeting role-play; learn about the 400-member House, the 24-member Senate, the Governor and Executive Council, and the Supreme Court; map Concord, Manchester, and your town.

g3_ss.title: New Hampshire's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: The Abenaki of N'dakinna: wigwams, the Three Sisters, maple sugaring, canoes, and Abenaki place names; Abenaki people in New Hampshire today.

g3_ss.title: New Hampshire Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Story cards for Passaconaway, Wentworth Cheswell, Prince Whipple, Ona Judge, Harriet Wilson, and Christa McAuliffe.

g45_ss.title: New Hampshire's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Pennacook, Squamscott, Cowasuck, and other Abenaki communities; Passaconaway and Wehanownowit; how the Wheelwright deed protected fishing rights.

g45_ss.title: Colony and Conflict
g45_ss.plan: Odiorne Point and Dover in 1623, disease and land loss, Waldron's 1676 trick and the 1689 attack on Dover, slavery in colonial Portsmouth, and the 1779 freedom petition.

g45_ss.title: Revolution, Constitution, and Civil War
g45_ss.plan: First state constitution (1776), the 1784 constitution, ratification as the ninth state, Ona Judge's escape, abolitionists like John P. Hale, and the Fighting Fifth.

g3_sci.title: Granite and Glaciers
g3_sci.plan: Look at granite up close and see how glaciers carved lakes, notches, and hills; why New Hampshire is the Granite State.

g3_sci.title: Maple Sugaring
g3_sci.plan: How trees make sap, why it runs in spring, and the 40-to-1 sap-to-syrup math.

g3_sci.title: Forest Animals
g3_sci.plan: Food webs with moose, black bears, purple finches, and salamanders in New Hampshire forests.

g45_sci.title: Mount Washington Weather
g45_sci.plan: Compare summit and valley weather data; explore wind, altitude, and why the summit has its own climate.

g45_sci.title: Weathering and the Old Man of the Mountain
g45_sci.plan: How freezing water and weather break down rock; investigate why the granite face fell in 2003.

g45_sci.title: Rivers, Mills, and Energy
g45_sci.plan: How the Merrimack's falls powered the Amoskeag mills; build a simple water wheel and discuss water power then and now.
